Closing — on reflection, `DEFAULT 0` (shipped in #26556) is the better behavior here.

`time_used` has exactly one reader: the recent-workspaces sort in `dialog-workspace-create.tsx`. Backfilling pre-existing rows to `unixepoch() * 1000` would cluster every migrated workspace at the top of the recent list with identical timestamps, drowning out real recent activity. Leaving them at `0` lets them surface naturally the next time someone opens a session in them (which bumps `time_used` to `Date.now()` via `projectors.ts`).

The original 'default to now instead of nullable' framing was based on a misread of the shipped fix — the column is already `NOT NULL DEFAULT 0`, not nullable.

> ## Stitch MCP - Bug Report: "Failed to get tools"
> ### Problem
> When configuring Google Stitch as a remote MCP server in opencode, the error "stitch Failed to get tools" appears and Stitch tools are not loaded.
> 
> ### Environment
> * opencode version: 1.14.33
> * OS: macOS
> * Stitch MCP endpoint: https://stitch.googleapis.com/mcp
> 
> ### Configuration
> {
>   "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
>   "mcp": {
>     "stitch": {
>       "type": "remote",
>       "url": "https://stitch.googleapis.com/mcp",
>       "enabled": true,
>       "headers": {
>         "X-Goog-Api-Key": "<API_KEY>"
>       }
>     }
>   }
> }
> ### What works
> * Direct curl to Stitch endpoint with POST returns tools correctly
> * The Stitch API responds correctly (405 on GET, 200 on POST with tools)
> 
> ### What doesn't work
> * opencode fails to load Stitch MCP tools despite API key being valid, config correct, and API responding properly to direct requests
> 
> ### Tested variations
> 1. Config with only Stitch MCP (no other providers/MCP servers) → Same error
> 2. Other remote MCP servers work fine with similar configuration
> 3. API key works via curl but not via opencode
> 
> ### Conclusion
> Bug in how opencode 1.14.33 handles the `X-Goog-Api-Key` header for remote MCP servers, or how it parses the response from Google's Stitch MCP endpoint.
> 
> ### Related Issues
> * [Agents and Commands are not shown #8868](https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/issues/8868) - Similar MCP remote server issues
> 
> ### Expected behavior
> Stitch MCP tools should be available in opencode when configured correctly.

```
name: opencode-review

on:
  pull_request:
    types: [opened, synchronize, reopened, ready_for_review]

jobs:
  review:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      id-token: write
      contents: read
      pull-requests: write
      issues: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: anomalyco/opencode/github@latest
        env:
          OPENCODE_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.OPENCODE_API_KEY }}
        with:
          model: opencode-go/kimi-k2.6
          prompt: |
            Review this pull request:
            - Check for code quality issues
            - Look for potential bugs
            - Suggest improvements
```

Checked #15555 and #20119. They are related, but I think this issue is a different request path.

Those issues describe SDK `client.session.prompt()` timing out while a Node SDK client waits for the OpenCode server response. This Desktop case uses the local Desktop/sidecar flow: the UI calls `prompt_async`, the local API returns immediately, and the long wait happens later when OpenCode's Node/Electron sidecar calls the OpenAI-compatible provider.

So the shared cause is Node/Undici's 300s `headersTimeout`, but the failing fetch is different:

- #15555 / #20119: SDK client -> OpenCode server
- this issue: OpenCode sidecar -> provider, e.g. Ollama

PR #26599 targets the provider fetch path in `packages/opencode/src/provider/provider.ts`, so it does not claim to close the SDK-client timeout issues.

Apologies — this issue was filed hastily without proper review. Unfortunately our bot (dorey-agent) doesn't have permission to edit the issue description or post comments on this repo, so we couldn't correct it earlier.

**The bug:** tool_call_update with status: "completed" sends part.state.title as title. For write/edit tools, that's the file path. The in_progress and error statuses correctly use part.tool (the actual tool name). This inconsistency causes ACP consumers to receive the file path as the tool identifier on completion.

Related: [#23947](tg://search_hashtag?hashtag=23947) proposes the opposite direction — using part.state.title for all statuses. Here's a comparison:

| Approach | Pros | Cons |
|----------|------|------|
| title: part.tool everywhere (this issue) | Consistent across statuses; consumers can rely on title for tool identity (emoji, grouping, dedup); semantic info still available in rawInput | Less descriptive title — consumers need to read rawInput for context |
| title: part.state.title everywhere ([#23947](tg://search_hashtag?hashtag=23947)) | Richer display label during running/pending | Consumers using title for tool identification break; duplicates info already in rawInput; mixes identity with description in one field |

Long-term, the cleanest solution would be separating name (tool identity, always part.tool) from title (semantic display label) at the protocol level. But as a minimal fix: keeping title as part.tool on all statuses preserves a clear contract for consumers, with rawInput as the source for richer context.

**Fix:** Lines 388 and 872 in packages/opencode/src/acp/agent.ts — change title: part.state.title to title: part.tool.

Since a couple of days or weeks, `opencode-cli.exe` is not even shipped with OpenCode Desktop anymore, so that it is necessary to download the CLI binary separately.

This would be fine-ish if OpenCode Desktop was features-complete in the sense that it could be used fully in standalone. But that's not the case: when you want to refresh the models list, you need the CLI. So basically OpenCode Desktop is currently a product with an expiration date: past a month or so, your install is outdated because you cannot refresh to get the latest models.

`opencode-cli.exe` should be reintegrated into OpenCode Desktop and renamed to `opencode.exe`, and the Desktop binary to `opencode-desktop.exe`.

After reviewing the proposal by @panwar-stack and the opencode-ensemble linked by @shahrin014 I believe people have become preoccupied with copying Claude Code Agent Teams, rather than trying to design an optimal environment for agents to collaborate autonomously while working tasks.

The basic premise of creating a set of tools an agent uses to create a team, send messages, and manage tasks is inefficient and counterproductive. The Agent Teams implementation by Anthropic was always generic and half-baked.

To get agents to work collaboratively means making a limited amount of harness native tools provide all needed functions. Not adding more and more tools to bloat context and degrade agent/model performance. The research data has been clear, adding more and more tools degrades agent performance - keep things lean and adaptable. Make a limited set of tools provide the functions needed under a wide variety of situations. Only make specific tools for critical functions that cannot be met through adapting the existing toolset. 

I'm still working on my Agentic Collaboration Framework, in which an 'agent teams equivalent or better' is naturally subsumed. It continues to be slow, challenging work, because it require a lot of thinking through the systems design. The implementation work is, trivial by comparison.

I spent over two months building a state modelling system, a type of specialized memory layer. I'm now working on refining a DCP fork I made in Jan-Feb into a a context management system that will enter into a feedback loop with the state modelling system, each enhancing an agents cognitive capabilities. Those systems will also benefit from any supplementary memory system; multiple feedback loops between complementary systems is the approach I'm taking. It's how biology works; it's innate to how complex systems operate.

Once agents have a state-modelling and context-management system, then a multi-caller system that enables agentic collaboration can be being driven by model intelligence alone. It'll practically self-assemble. I'm already seeing that occur in my state-model system - the agents are collecting performance data on tasked agents, compiling the data, using it to construct models about each AI models performance on the tasks in the projects, and then injecting guidance into the orchestrating agents context. 

Most of the wiring in these Agent Team copy-cat plugins create logic that is unnecessary, even counterproductive. Most of the core functions of 'Agent Teams' can be obtained by making agent-skills while using my OpenCode PR that lets subagents task subagents and persist subagent sessions. 

Claude Code needed Agent Teams instead of an Agent Skill because Claude Code does not allow you to persist subagent session and have subagent task and persist other subagents. If you really want Agents to collaborate, you do not use 'Agent Teams'. You create a harness native environment where collaboration is an organic process that occurs in response to task complexity.

Rather than having a plugin with tons of added tools, there is a more elegant solution using the Task tool and an agent skill, loaded only when a task is complex enough to require multi-agent orchestration. The Natural Language code of an agent-skill is easily transferable and can rapidly iterate, and can benefit from a wider range of human expertise during development. The same is not true of these plugins. 

People need to put a lot more thought into the systems design. It's the hard part, and it's what Anthropic seems to suck the most at when it comes to Claude Code development.

**Key differences:**

1. **Type:** #23996 is a user bug report ("server breaks after hours"); #26646 is a **feature request** for crash resilience improvements
2. **Root cause hypothesis:** #23996 suspects memory leak (`RADAR_PRE_LEAK_64` + EPERM errors); #26646 identifies **file watcher storms (6,030 events/min)** + **watchdog degradation** as the primary mechanism
3. **Data depth:** #26646 provides quantitative analysis — 28 crashes over 3 days, 150K file watcher events, hourly breakdown showing 5x log volume spikes
4. **Unique finding in #26646:** The **auto-recovery watchdog degradation** pattern — on May 7, `Module loaded` followed `session.error` within 1-3 minutes; from May 8 onward, 15 consecutive errors had zero auto-restarts (server dead for 9 hours). #23996 does not address auto-recovery at all
5. **Scope:** #26646 proposes specific enhancements: error detail logging, file watcher exclusion patterns, debouncing, watchdog process, session rate-limiting, health endpoint — none of which are in #23996

### vs #25883 (File watcher → zombie processes on macOS)

**Overlaps:**
- Both recognize excessive file watcher activity as a server resource problem

**Key differences:**

1. **Platform:** #25883 is **macOS-specific** (zombie child reaping in `cross-spawn-spawner.ts`); #26646 is **Windows-specific** with no zombie process involvement
2. **Impact:** #25883 documents high CPU/system load from zombie management; #26646 documents **server crashes** (28 times) and **session.error events** — the end-to-end crash cycle
3. **Mechanism:** #25883 focuses on libuv `SIGCHLD` reaping backpressure; #26646 covers the full chain: file storm → resource exhaustion → session crash → no auto-recovery
4. **Feature requests overlap:** Both touch on debouncing file events, but #26646 additionally requests: watchdog auto-restart, error detail logging, exclude patterns config, session rate-limiting, and a health endpoint — none in #25883

### Summary

#26646 is best understood as a **feature request** that connects three dots found across separate issues:
1. File watcher resource pressure (also seen in #25883)
2. Server crashes with session.error (also seen in #23996)
3. **Missing crash auto-recovery** (unique to #26646)

The third point — that the server had working auto-restart on day 1 which then silently degraded — is the most actionable finding and not covered by either existing issue.

In my case the root cause turned out to be a combination of two things:

1. tmux intercepting modified keys — I had legacy bind-key -n S-Enter send-keys C-j and user-keys bindings in .tmux.conf that converted Shift+Enter into Ctrl+J. This worked with older OpenCode versions where C-j was mapped to newline, but the new keymap engine (@opentui/keymap) no longer treats C-j as input_newline by default. The fix was to remove those tmux bindings entirely and let the modified key sequences pass through to OpenCode natively.

2. Silent config rejection — confirming what's already reported here: any unrecognized key in keybinds causes the entire tui.json to be silently ignored, so even valid bindings like input_newline stop working with no warning. Removing the custom keybinds block and relying on the built-in defaults restored newline functionality immediately.For anyone running OpenCode inside tmux: check that your .tmux.conf isn't transforming Shift+Enter / Ctrl+Enter / Alt+Enter into something else. The new engine handles these natively — no conversion needed.

Since opening this PR, the underlying issue has been confirmed by two more users on different providers:

- **Databricks** ([@jairbubbles](https://github.com/jairbubbles) in #25984): Databricks model serving also expects `cache_control: { type: "ephemeral" }` in `messages.content` blocks — the same mechanism this fix implements. [Their docs confirm it.](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/machine-learning/model-serving/score-foundation-models#prompt-cache)
- **Xiaomi Mimo direct API** ([@xenstar](https://github.com/xenstar) in #25984): Without the fix, there is zero caching and credits burn rapidly. With OpenRouter (which handles the translation itself), the same model hits ~95% cache rate.

This makes it clear the issue affects a broad class of OpenAI-compatible proxies that route to Anthropic-capable backends — not just Bifrost/LiteLLM. The `cacheStrategy: "bedrock"` approach this PR introduces generalises cleanly to all of them.

The fix is minimal and isolated to `transform.ts` with a guard that keeps the existing `applyCaching()` path completely unchanged for native providers. Happy to address any review feedback.
